source.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: David Chanin; James Wilken-Smith; Tomás Dulka; Hardik Bhatnagar; Satvik Golechha; J. Bloom

page_placements.theme: SAE latents become polysemantic through absorption, hedging and co-occurrence

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The text gives an arXiv v6 date of 17 Nov 2025 and identifies the paper as NeurIPS 2025, while the supplied metadata says year 2024.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests feature absorption in sparse-autoencoder latents, not polysemanticity of individual neurons or any of the claim versions' specified neuron-level behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper reports substantial results on SAE latents, including a toy hierarchy, an LLM spelling case study, and aggregate absorption-rate plots. These bear on SAE feature interpretation, a related but different construct; they are recorded as findings about the claim's subject with versions ["none"]. The paper also discusses superposition as background, but does not test polysemanticity of neurons.
record.test_reason: The study measures feature absorption in sparse-autoencoder latents on Gemma-2-2B, Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2 0.5B. It also uses toy SAEs and a proof. Superposition and polysemantic neurons appear only as background motivation. No result measures how often individual model neurons respond to unrelated inputs, what causes that, or how architecture or measurement choices change it. SAE-latent false negatives are a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state that varying SAE size or sparsity is insufficient to solve absorption. They say absorption occurs in every LLM SAE they tested, and they frame it as a fundamental limitation of sparse feature extraction.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies SAE feature absorption rather than the original claim's neuron polysemanticity; it does not reproduce the cited neuron studies.
record.method_sensitivity: For SAE-latent measurements, absorption rates vary with L0 and SAE width; the authors report no obvious layer pattern. Their estimated rates also depend on metric choices and thresholds.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy SAEs, hierarchically co-occurring features led the SAE to omit the parent feature on child cases and to merge the parent direction into the child latent. Independent features were recovered cleanly. The same holds for TopK SAEs and for imperfect co-occurrence (partial absorption).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE sparsity optimization produces feature absorption when features form a hierarchy.

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma Scope layer-3 latent 6510 ('starts with S', F1 0.81) fails to fire on _short. Token-aligned latent 1085 carries the causally relevant first-letter direction instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seemingly monosemantic SAE latents can have arbitrary false negatives because more specific latents absorb their feature.

fits_no_version.finding: Absorption occurs in Gemma Scope, Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2 0.5B SAEs. Its rate rises with SAE width and sparsity, with no clear layer pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature absorption is widespread across LLM SAEs, and varying SAE size or sparsity does not remove it.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025), as stated in the paper text
record.problems: The absorption metric cannot establish causal absorption beyond layer 17 in Gemma-2-2B for this task, requires a dominant single absorbing latent, and misses cases where main latents fire weakly or multiple latents absorb together. The authors describe the metric as a conservative underestimate; thresholds were selected by manual inspection. They also report training only a small number of non-JumpReLU SAEs due to compute constraints. Aggregate rate values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows were applicable. The paper reports other SAE classification, feature-splitting, and editing results, but they do not test neuron polysemanticity or the behaviors named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons studied.
No measurement of MLP neuron polysemanticity in language models; only residual-stream SAE latents.
Superposition is cited as background only. The paper does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by packing sparse features.
Initialization, regularization or noise as causes of polysemantic neurons are not studied.
Activation function and architecture effects on the share of polysemantic neurons are not measured. SAE L1 vs TopK comparisons concern absorption, not neurons.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
Measurement-dependence of neuron polysemanticity labels is not studied. Metric-choice sensitivity is shown only for the SAE absorption metric.

record.verdict_notes: Relation could arguably be 'assumes': the introduction takes superposition as the reason neurons are hard to interpret. However, no neuron-level result is reported. R4 and R5 come from the same figure and could be merged. Peer-review status (NeurIPS 2025) is taken from the paper text.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and the InceptionV1 examples are not studied.
The study measures SAE latents, not MLP neurons responding to unrelated language-model tokens or contexts.
The study argues that hierarchical co-occurrence and sparsity cause absorption in SAE latents; it does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Initialization, regularization, or training noise causing polysemantic neurons without capacity pressure is not tested.
The study compares SAE absorption behavior, including L1 and TopK SAEs, but does not measure neuron polysemanticity or whether its share can be lowered without a large performance loss.
The study investigates SAE latents and absorbed task information, not whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs.
The study varies SAE-based classification and absorption metrics, not how measurement choices determine whether neurons count as polysemantic.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained an SAE on independently firing toy features.
rows.measure: Recovery of the toy features by SAE encoder and decoder
rows.value: The SAE perfectly recovered the features, learning one latent per true feature.
rows.note: Control condition for the hierarchical co-occurrence toy experiment; this is an SAE feature-recovery result, not a neuron polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained an SAE on toy features where feature 1 fires only when feature 0 fires.
rows.measure: Whether the SAE encoder and decoder recover the toy features separately
rows.value: Latent 0 omitted feature 1 cases; latent 1 absorbed the feature 0 direction. Features 2 and 3 remained independently represented.
rows.note: The authors also provide an analytical argument that absorption reduces sparsity loss under their specified hierarchy assumptions.

rows.subject: Gemma Scope layer 3, 16k width, 59 L0 SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE-latent classification and causal contribution on a first-letter task.

conditions.value: predict first letter of a token

rows.measure: First-letter classification and causal contribution to the model's first-letter behavior
rows.baseline: The main “starts with S” latent 6510 activates for most tested S-starting tokens.
rows.value: Latent 6510 had F1 0.81 but did not activate on _short; token-aligned latent 1085 activated instead. Latent 1085 had cosine similarity 0.12 with the “starts with S” probe versus 0.52 for latent 6510, and the paper reports that its activation magnitude on _short was about 5 times that of latent 6510. Ablating 1085 had the largest effect; removing its probe component eliminated its significant ablation effect.
rows.note: This is evidence about SAE-latent absorption on the spelling task, not about polysemantic neurons.

rows.subject: Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs on Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Estimated feature absorption rate across SAE L0 settings.
rows.value: figure only; the authors state absorption rate increases with higher sparsity.
rows.note: The absorption metric requires causal ablation evidence and is limited to layers 0-17 for this analysis.

relation.reason: Superposition and polysemantic activations come up only as background motivation (intro, lines 53-60). 'discusses' fits.

tranche.reason: The paper measures SAE feature absorption, not neuron polysemanticity. It neither tests nor uses the claim.

source_check.notes: The rows are SAE-latent absorption evidence and are not linked to any claim version. Figure 9 values are figure-only. Width/sparsity trends are for Gemma Scope only. The Llama/Qwen SAEs are the authors' own; A.9 gives their L0 but not their width.

statements.correction: Facts: latent 6510 F1 0.81, no activation on _short; latent 1085 absorbs the direction (ablation, Fig 7); absorption rate rises with SAE width and sparsity (Gemma Scope 16k/65k, layers 0-17); absorption also seen in the authors' Llama 3.2 1B (L1, TopK) and Qwen2 0.5B (L1) SAEs.
statements.problem: All of it is in the text: the Gemma Scope layer 3 (16k, L0 59) latent 6510 has F1 0.81 and does not fire on _short, and latent 1085 (cos 0.12 with the probe) causally carries the 'starts with S' direction. Absorption appears in Gemma Scope, Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2 0.5B SAEs. The rise with width and sparsity was measured on Gemma Scope only (Fig 9b). The paper states this trend in general terms, so the wording is acceptable.
